notes: House of Saud is the ruling slot 10 (MD sprite). Hashemites kept at 0 per MD. Royal factions: Sudairi Seven at 23 (dynastic bloc distinct from the ruling house), Abdullah's National Guard at 14. The 1970 communist party is the National Liberation Front (renamed Saudi Communist Party only in 1975), placed in the pro-Soviet slot 4; slot 19 holds the Marxist-turning Saudi ANM branch. Muslim World League fills 12 (Brotherhood exiles), JSM fills 11. Ba'ath kept at 21 per MD.

0.name: Al-Hashimiyyun
0.text:
The House of Hashim ruled the Hijaz for centuries as Sharifs of Mecca and as kings from 1916 until Ibn Saud's conquest of 1925. Driven out to Jordan and Iraq, the family lost Baghdad in 1958 but still reigns in Amman, where King Hussein heads the dynasty and remains a close partner of Britain and the United States.

In the Hijaz, Sharifian sentiment lingers among some ashraf families of Mecca and Medina and among townsmen who remember a more cosmopolitan pre-Saudi order. The Hashemites stand for pro-Western dynastic authoritarianism resting on descent from the Prophet. Their leverage is limited to lineage, memory and the alliance of conservative monarchies against Nasserism and communism.

1.name: Rijal al-Naft
1.text:
The Oil Men are the Western-educated technocrats who manage the kingdom's petroleum wealth, led by Ahmed Zaki Yamani, a Meccan lawyer trained at New York University and Harvard and Minister of Petroleum since 1962. Around him stand the managers of Petromin, the state petroleum agency, and the graduates of the College of Petroleum and Minerals in Dhahran.

They are loyal to King Faisal, conservative in religion and close to Washington, but believe the state must gain control of its oil step by step through 'participation' in Aramco rather than through nationalisation. They favour planning, education and gradual modernisation under the monarchy. Their leverage is expertise: no one else can negotiate with the oil majors.

2.name: Harakat al-Umara' al-Ahrar
2.text:
The Free Princes Movement was formed in 1958 by Prince Talal bin Abdulaziz and several of his half-brothers, among them Badr and Fawwaz, to demand a constitution and an elected assembly. Exiled to Cairo in 1962 and dubbed the 'Red Princes', they made their peace with Faisal in 1964. The movement is formally disbanded, but Talal remains its unrepentant symbol.

The Free Princes stand for a constitutional monarchy, a written basic law, a consultative council with elected members, equal citizenship and modern education. They are pro-Western in economics but sympathetic to Arab nationalism. Their leverage lies in royal blood, contacts among Hijazi professionals and the unkept promise of reform in Faisal's 1962 programme.

3.name: Lajnat al-'Ummal
3.text:
The Workers' Committee is the underground network of Saudi employees of Aramco and the oil-service firms in Dhahran, Ras Tanura and Abqaiq, heir to the committees that led the great strikes of 1953 and 1956. Strikes and unions are banned by royal decree and its veterans were jailed or deported, yet it survives in informal circles of drillers, clerks and drivers.

It demands decent wages, housing and promotion for Saudis, an end to privileges for American staff and the right to organise; the 1969 Labour Law answers only part of this. Moderate in tone and wary of communist slogans, it seeks reform through the company and the government. Its leverage is the oil fields themselves.

4.name: Jabhat al-Tahrir al-Watani
4.text:
The National Liberation Front is Saudi Arabia's clandestine communist party, founded in 1958 out of the National Reform Front that grew among Aramco workers after the 1953 strike. Its members are oil workers, teachers, Shia activists from the Eastern Province and students abroad; many were seized in the sweeping arrests of 1969, and its exiled cadres organise from abroad.

The Front demands the overthrow of the monarchy, nationalisation of Aramco, land reform, trade-union rights and the removal of American military missions. It follows the Soviet line, praising Moscow as the ally of Arab liberation. Its leverage lies in disciplined cells inside the oil industry and in the backing of the international communist movement.

5.name: Jil al-Naksa
5.text:
The Generation of the Setback is the radicalised youth of the kingdom: students in Beirut, Cairo and the United States, young teachers and technicians who saw the defeat of June 1967 as the bankruptcy of every Arab government. They read Guevara, Mao and Fanon, cheer the fedayeen and the Dhofar rebels, and drift away from the older nationalist parties.

They reject monarchy, oil-company paternalism and Soviet-style caution alike, calling for armed popular revolution across the Arabian Peninsula. Organisationally weak and watched by the Mabahith, they meet in study circles and act through Palestinian and Gulf revolutionary groups. Their leverage lies in their education and the restlessness of a growing student population.

6.name: Hay'at al-Amr bi-l-Ma'ruf wa-l-Nahy 'an al-Munkar
6.english: Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice
6.text:
The Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, the religious police known as the mutawwa'in, patrols streets and markets in Riyadh, Mecca and the towns of Najd, enforcing attendance at prayer, modest dress and the closing of shops at prayer time. Rooted in the Wahhabi ulama, it is directed by members of the Al ash-Sheikh family.

The committees are the backbone of resistance to imported mores: they have opposed television, cinemas, music and girls' schools, and see Western engineers, films and fashions as a moral invasion. Hostile to Western culture rather than to the dynasty, they demand a stricter Islamic order. Their leverage is the street, the mosque and the ulama's veto over Faisal's reforms.
6.wiki: Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice (Saudi Arabia)

7.name: Dubbat Haziran
7.text:
The June Officers are the remnants of the military conspiracy uncovered in June 1969, when the regime arrested scores of air force and army officers and civilian sympathisers accused of plotting a republican coup. Many came from the Hijaz and the new technical branches; survivors in the ranks keep silent, but the network has not been fully destroyed.

Inspired by Nasser's Egypt and by the officers who seized power in Iraq, Yemen and, most recently, Libya, they dream of an Arab republic run by the army, with oil nationalised, the royal family removed and foreign advisers expelled. They look to Cairo and, through it, to Moscow. Their leverage lies in uniforms, weapons and the example of the Libyan revolution.

8.name: Wujaha' al-Qatif
8.text:
The Notables of Qatif are the merchant families, Ja'fari judges and traditional clerics who speak for the Shia of the Eastern Province, concentrated in the oases of Qatif and al-Ahsa. They follow the great marja' of Najaf, Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim, and negotiate quietly with the provincial governor and with Aramco, which employs many Shia workers.

They seek tolerance rather than power: freedom to build husayniyyas and hold Ashura processions, recognition of Ja'fari courts, a fair share of jobs, schooling and public posts, and an end to anti-Shia polemics by Wahhabi preachers. Outwardly loyal to the crown, they bargain from the strategic position of a community living on top of the kingdom's oil.

9.name: Talabat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Students of Najaf are young Saudi Shia seminarians and returnees from the shrine cities of Iraq, where they meet the activist ideas of the Islamic Da'wa Party and of Ayatollah Muhammad al-Shirazi's circle in Karbala. Back in Qatif and al-Ahsa, they run discreet study circles in husayniyyas and private homes.

They reject the quietism of their elders and the legitimacy of a Wahhabi monarchy that treats Shiism as heresy, and dream of an Islamic order guided by militant clerics. Hostile to American oil power and atheist communism alike, they are still few and closely watched. Their leverage lies in religious networks and the grievances of a marginalised community.

10.name: Al Sa'ud
10.text:
The House of Saud has ruled the kingdom since Abdulaziz ibn Saud unified it in 1932, governing through the alliance with the Wahhabi ulama first sealed in 1744. King Faisal bin Abdulaziz, who replaced his brother Saud in 1964, is both king and prime minister, with Crown Prince Khalid at his side.

Faisal rules as a cautious modernizer and pan-Islamic statesman: he has abolished slavery, opened girls' schools and introduced television, while presenting the kingdom as Islam's guardian against Zionism and atheist communism. After the al-Aqsa fire he championed the Rabat Islamic summit of September 1969. The dynasty's leverage is oil revenue, the ulama, the National Guard and its alliance with the United States.

11.name: Al-Jama'a al-Salafiyya al-Muhtasiba
11.english: Salafi Group That Commands Right and Forbids Wrong
11.text:
The Salafi Group That Commands Right and Forbids Wrong was founded in Medina in the mid-1960s by young students of hadith determined to return Islam to its original purity. Sheikh Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz of the Islamic University of Medina has given it his blessing, and it spreads through study circles, preaching tours and volunteers who confront what they call innovations.

The group rejects the compromises of the official ulama, distrusts the royal family's Western friends and its modern bureaucracy, and condemns photography, television and foreign customs. Its members, many from Bedouin and National Guard families, form a seedbed for millenarian and anti-state ideas. Its leverage is zeal and moral authority among the pious.

12.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
12.text:
The Muslim World League was founded in Mecca in 1962 at Saudi initiative as the pan-Islamic answer to Nasser's revolutionary Arabism. Its Secretary-General, the Hijazi statesman Muhammad Surur al-Sabban, presides over a council of scholars from across the Muslim world, while exiled Egyptian and Syrian Muslim Brothers staff its offices, journals and missions.

The League promotes Islamic solidarity, mosque building, missionary work and the Islamisation of education, and campaigns against communism, secular nationalism and Zionism. Through it the Brotherhood's activist ideas are spreading in Saudi universities. Its leverage lies in royal funds, global networks of preachers and students, and Faisal's ambition to lead the Islamic world.

13.name: Hay'at al-Takhtit al-Markaziyya
13.text:
The Central Planning Organization is the kingdom's planning bureaucracy, headed since 1968 by Hisham Nazer, a young Hijazi technocrat educated at the University of California. With American advisers it is completing the first Five-Year Development Plan, meant to turn oil revenues into roads, ports, schools, hospitals and industry from 1970 onward.

The planners believe in administration rather than politics: no parties and no parliament, but rational budgets, trained Saudi cadres and a modern civil service under the king's authority. They borrow freely from Western expertise while staying out of bloc rivalries. Their leverage lies in budgets, statistics and the ministries that depend on them, and in Faisal's personal confidence.

14.name: Al-Haras al-Watani
14.text:
The Saudi Arabian National Guard is the tribal army of the dynasty, commanded since 1962 by Prince Abdullah bin Abdulaziz. Recruited from loyal Najdi tribes, many of them sons of the Ikhwan warriors of the 1920s, and trained with British help, it guards the royal family, the oil fields and the cities and balances the regular army.

Abdullah's Guard is conservative, pious and Bedouin in spirit, with an Arab nationalist streak that makes its commander cooler toward Washington than his Sudairi half-brothers and warmer toward the Arab republics. It favours tribal patronage, subsidies and consensus among the princes. Its leverage lies in armed loyalty and Abdullah's place in the line of succession.

15.name: Arabian American Oil Company
15.text:
The Arabian American Oil Company holds the concession for nearly all of the kingdom's oil and is owned by four American majors: Standard Oil of New Jersey, Standard Oil of California, Texaco and Mobil. From its headquarters in Dhahran it pumps millions of barrels a day, runs its own towns, schools and hospitals, and pays the royalties and taxes that fund the Saudi state.

Aramco stands for American private enterprise, long-term concessions and close ties between Riyadh and Washington. It resists Yamani's demands for participation, trains a loyal Saudi managerial class and keeps a careful eye on labour and Shia unrest. Its leverage is immense: oil, money, expertise and a direct line to the State Department.

16.name: Al-Ghurfa al-Tijariyya al-Sina'iyya bi-Jidda
16.english: Jeddah Chamber of Commerce and Industry
16.text:
The Jeddah Chamber of Commerce and Industry, founded in 1946 as the first chamber in the kingdom, speaks for the great Hijazi merchant houses of the Red Sea port, among them the Alirezas, Juffalis, Zahids and Kakis: holders of foreign agencies, importers and financiers of the pilgrimage trade.

The merchants want free trade, low duties, protection of commercial agencies, light regulation and a state that buys from private firms instead of competing with them. Socially conservative but cosmopolitan, they favour Western partners and distrust both socialist planning and Najdi bureaucrats. Their leverage lies in the import trade, the Hajj economy and the loans they extend to princes.

17.name: Ahl al-Hima
17.text:
The People of the Hima are Bedouin elders, highland villagers of Asir and the Hijaz and a handful of foresters and agronomists in the Ministry of Agriculture who mourn the ruin of the kingdom's pastures. The ancient hima reserves, protected grazing lands held by tribes and villages, were largely thrown open by the state in the 1950s, and motorised hunting is wiping out the oryx and gazelle.

They call for restoring protected grazing, controlling wells and herds, planting trees and banning hunting from cars, blending Islamic stewardship of creation with tribal custom. With no organisation and few patrons beyond some officials, their leverage lies in the authority of elders and the visible advance of the desert.

18.name: Ittihad Sha'b al-Jazira al-'Arabiyya
18.english: Union of the People of the Arabian Peninsula
18.text:
The Union of the People of the Arabian Peninsula was founded in 1959 by Nasser al-Said, a Shammari from Ha'il and veteran of the 1953 Aramco strike, who has led it from exile ever since. Backed by Cairo during the Yemen war, it broadcast fierce attacks on the House of Saud, but Nasser's reconciliation with Faisal at Khartoum in 1967 has left it short of patrons.

The Union calls for a republic, a constitution, Arab unity and Arab socialism: nationalised oil, land reform, free education and the end of American influence. It looks to Nasser's Egypt and revolutionary South Yemen. Its leverage lies in exile networks, radio propaganda and sympathisers among officers and workers.

19.name: Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-'Arab
19.text:
The Arab Nationalist Movement's Saudi branch was built in the 1960s by students, teachers and Aramco employees who followed George Habash's pan-Arab movement. Since the 1967 defeat the movement has turned toward Marxism and is breaking into national parties across the Arab world; in Saudi Arabia its cadres were rounded up in the mass arrests of 1969.

The surviving members reject both the monarchy and Soviet-style communism, advocating a scientific socialism adapted to Arab conditions, solidarity with the PFLP and the Dhofar revolution, and a people's war against imperialism across the Gulf. Their leverage lies in clandestine cells in the Eastern Province and the Hijaz and in ties to comrades in Kuwait, Bahrain and Aden.

20.name: Abna' al-Hijaz
20.text:
The Sons of the Hijaz are the townsmen of Mecca, Medina, Jeddah and Taif who resent Najdi domination of the state that conquered their kingdom in 1925: pilgrim guides of the mutawwif guilds, shopkeepers, minor clerks and the sons of old families passed over for promotion. They remember the Hijaz Kingdom and the Hijaz National Party of 1924.

Their mood is populist rather than ideological: Hijazi pride, cosmopolitan tolerance against Wahhabi zeal, and anger at princely privilege, monopolies and officials sent from Riyadh. They want a fair share of jobs, local councils and respect for Hijazi customs. Their leverage lies in the Hajj economy and the many Hijazis in the bureaucracy.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
The Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party has kept a small clandestine branch in the kingdom since the 1950s, recruited among students, teachers, officers and Arab expatriates. Torn by the 1966 split between the rival commands in Damascus and Baghdad, it lost many members in the arrests of 1969, and its exiles look increasingly to the new Ba'athist regime in Iraq.

The Ba'athists call for Arab unity, freedom and socialism under a single vanguard party, an end to the monarchy and the use of oil wealth for the whole Arab nation. They are militaristic, conspiratorial and fiercely anti-Western. Their leverage lies in Iraqi money and training, and in sympathisers inside the armed forces.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Sa'udiyya
22.text:
The Saudi Arabian Armed Forces, comprising the army, the air force and a small navy, are run by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz, Minister of Defence and Aviation since 1962. Trained by American and British missions, the air force is taking delivery of British Lightning fighters, and a Saudi brigade has been stationed in Jordan since the 1967 war.

The officer corps is professional, pampered and closely watched; the 1969 plot showed the regime that technical branches breed radical ideas. Most officers stand for order, loyalty to the king and partnership with the West, but resent princely interference in promotions. Their leverage lies in weapons, the defence budget and their role as the last guarantor of the throne.

23.name: Al-Sudayriyyun al-Sab'a
23.text:
The Sudairi Seven are the full brothers born to King Abdulaziz by Hassa bint Ahmad al-Sudairi, the most cohesive bloc within the royal family. Prince Fahd, Minister of Interior and second deputy prime minister, leads them; Sultan holds Defence, Salman governs Riyadh, and Abdul Rahman, Nayef, Turki and Ahmed hold lesser posts.

The brothers stand for a strong, centralised monarchy, modernisation from above, a tough internal security service and a firm alliance with the United States against Nasserism and communism. They aim to secure the succession after Faisal and Khalid for their own line. Their leverage lies in the ministries they control, their unity and their close American relationships.
